questions.stem: A patient with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) is most likely to have which of the following autoantibodies?
explanations: Incorrect. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with diffuse disease and increased risk of rapidly progressive skin involvement and renal crisis, not limited/CREST disease.
Incorrect. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with polymyositis, not scleroderma.
Incorrect. Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis, not the limited/CREST form.
Correct. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is associated with limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome)—centromere corresponds to the 'C' in CREST as a mnemonic.
questions.overview: Systemic sclerosis presents in diffuse (early visceral organ involvement, associated with anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, risk of renal crisis) and limited/CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias; associated with anti-centromere antibody) forms. Limited disease generally has a more benign course, with pulmonary hypertension and interstitial lung disease as the leading causes of death.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes T-cell-independent B-cell activation?
options: Occurs only within the thymic medulla
Triggered by non-protein antigens such as bacterial polysaccharides, producing mainly IgM with no memory cell formation
Produces predominantly IgG antibodies with a robust memory response
Requires antigen presentation via MHC class II and CD40-CD40L interaction, producing class-switched antibodies
explanations: Incorrect. B-cell activation occurs in secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen), not the thymic medulla, which is a site of T-cell negative selection.

Correct. T-cell-independent activation is triggered by non-protein antigens (e.g., polysaccharide capsules, LPS), producing a relatively weak response that is mostly IgM with no memory B cells generated.
Incorrect. T-cell-independent activation produces mostly IgM, not class-switched IgG, and does not generate memory cells; that profile describes T-cell-dependent activation instead.

Incorrect. This describes T-cell-dependent activation, which requires protein antigens, MHC class II presentation to T cells, and CD40-CD40L interaction, resulting in class switching and memory formation.
questions.overview: B cells can be activated by T-cell-dependent (protein antigen, requires MHC II/CD40-CD40L/B7-CD28 interactions with T cells, produces class switching and memory) or T-cell-independent (non-protein antigens like bacterial polysaccharides, weaker response, mostly IgM, no memory) pathways. This distinction underlies the rationale for conjugate vaccines, which link polysaccharide antigens to protein carriers to recruit T-cell help.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old boy presents with recurrent otitis media and pneumonia, widespread eczema, and easy bruising with petechiae. Laboratory studies reveal thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and elevated serum IgE and IgA levels. This condition is caused by a defect in a gene responsible for which of the following?
options: Bruton tyrosine kinase required for B-cell precursor maturation
Expression of self-antigens in the thymic medulla for negative selection
The gamma subunit of the interleukin-2 receptor
Maintenance of the T-cell cytoskeleton required for immunologic synapse formation
explanations: Incorrect. Lysosomal trafficking regulator gene mutations cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome, characterized by recurrent infections and albinism, not eczema and thrombocytopenia.
Incorrect. Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, which presents with absent B cells and recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections but not eczema or thrombocytopenia.
Incorrect. Defective expression of self-antigens in the thymic medulla describes AIRE gene mutations, causing chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with endocrinopathy, not this presentation.
Incorrect. Mutation of the IL-2 receptor gamma chain (IL2RG) causes X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which lacks the eczema/thrombocytopenia triad described.

Correct. This is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked disorder of the WAS gene; the resulting WAS protein (WASp) is necessary for T-cell cytoskeletal maintenance and immunologic synapse formation, producing the triad of immune dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, and eczema, often with elevated IgE and IgA.
questions.overview: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by mutation of the WAS gene, whose protein product is required for T-cell cytoskeletal function and immunologic synapse formation with antigen-presenting cells. Classic presentation is a male infant around 6 months of age with the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia (bleeding/petechiae), and recurrent infections, often with elevated IgE and IgA.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and dark urine for the past week, following a recent respiratory illness. His blood pressure is elevated. Urinalysis reveals hematuria with red cell casts, and his creatinine is elevated. A renal biopsy shows linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence. Antibodies in this condition are directed against which of the following structures?
options: Alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
explanations: Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are seen in SLE and are associated with lupus nephritis, which shows granular (not linear) immune complex deposition, not the linear pattern described here.

Correct. Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen (anti-GBM), found in both the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, producing hemoptysis and nephritic syndrome with linear IgG/C3 deposition on immunofluorescence.
Incorrect. Antibodies against desmosomal proteins cause pemphigus vulgaris, a skin blistering disease, not pulmonary-renal disease.
Incorrect. Antibodies against acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular disorder, not hemoptysis and nephritis.
Incorrect. Rheumatoid factor targets the Fc portion of IgG in rheumatoid arthritis; this is unrelated to the anti-GBM disease described here.
questions.overview: Goodpasture syndrome is a type II hypersensitivity disease caused by antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, producing the classic combination of hemoptysis and nephritic syndrome (hematuria) in a young adult male. Immunofluorescence shows a characteristic linear pattern of IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane.

questions.stem: A medication used for acute gout flares works by binding tubulin and preventing microtubule polymerization, thereby inhibiting neutrophil migration and phagocytosis. This describes which drug?
explanations: Incorrect. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases uric acid production; it does not affect microtubules.
Correct. Colchicine is a microtubule inhibitor that binds tubulin, preventing polymerization into microtubules and thereby inhibiting neutrophil migration and phagocytosis during acute gout attacks.
Incorrect. Febuxostat is a non-competitive xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for chronic urate lowering, not a microtubule inhibitor.
Incorrect. Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that promotes renal excretion of uric acid; it does not inhibit microtubule function.
questions.overview: Colchicine is a microtubule inhibitor used for acute gout attacks (as well as pericarditis and familial Mediterranean fever), working by binding tubulin to block neutrophil migration and phagocytosis. Its main adverse effects are gastrointestinal (diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain).

questions.stem: A patient receives a tetanus toxoid booster injection and develops localized swelling, redness, and pain at the injection site 6 hours later. Biopsy would most likely show immune complex and complement deposition in the vessel walls. This reaction is best classified as which type of hypersensitivity?
explanations: Incorrect. Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies directly targeting cell-surface or tissue antigens, not immune complex deposition in vessel walls.

Correct. This is an Arthus reaction, a localized type III hypersensitivity reaction that occurs 4-10 hours after antigen injection (e.g., tetanus, diphtheria, hepatitis B vaccines) due to local immune complex formation and complement activation, causing edema and necrosis.
Incorrect. Type I hypersensitivity occurs within minutes of antigen exposure via IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, not hours later with immune complex/complement deposition.

Incorrect. Type IV hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated and typically occurs 24-72 hours after exposure without antibody or complement involvement, unlike the immune complex/complement pattern described here.
questions.overview: The Arthus reaction is a localized type III hypersensitivity response occurring hours after antigen injection into a person with preformed circulating antibodies, producing local immune complex formation, complement activation, edema, and tissue necrosis. It is distinguished from generalized type III disease (serum sickness) by its localized nature and from type I reactions by its delayed (hours, not minutes) onset.

questions.stem: A gene expressed in the thymic medulla promotes presentation of self-antigens to developing T cells, leading to apoptosis of strongly self-reactive clones (negative selection). Mutation of this gene causes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with endocrine dysfunction. This gene is:
explanations: Incorrect. IL2RG mutations cause X-linked SCID due to defective cytokine receptor signaling, not a defect of thymic self-antigen presentation.

Correct. AIRE promotes expression of self-antigens by thymic medullary epithelial cells and dendritic cells for negative selection; its mutation causes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (via defective Dectin-1-mediated response to Candida) along with autoimmune endocrine dysfunction (hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency).
Incorrect. WAS mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, affecting T-cell cytoskeletal function, not thymic negative selection via self-antigen presentation.
Incorrect. BTK mutations cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a B-cell maturation defect, not a thymic negative selection defect.
questions.overview: In the thymus, positive selection (cortex) tests T cells for binding to self MHC, while negative selection (medulla) eliminates T cells that bind too strongly to self-antigens, a process promoted by the AIRE gene, which drives ectopic expression of self-antigens by medullary epithelial and dendritic cells. AIRE mutations cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with associated hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency due to both loss of Candida defense and autoimmune destruction of endocrine glands.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with known diffuse systemic sclerosis (skin thickening of the trunk and proximal extremities, Raynaud phenomenon) presents with a severe headache and blurred vision. Blood pressure is 210/125 mmHg, and her creatinine has risen sharply from baseline. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanations: Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is used for vasculitides and severe glomerulonephritis but is not the standard treatment for scleroderma renal crisis.
Incorrect. Immunosuppressants such as corticosteroids have limited proven benefit in systemic sclerosis and are not the treatment for the acute hypertensive renal crisis.

Correct. This presentation is scleroderma renal crisis, a life-threatening complication of diffuse systemic sclerosis characterized by malignant hypertension and acute renal failure; it classically responds to ACE inhibitors.
Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers are used for Raynaud phenomenon in scleroderma, not specifically indicated for scleroderma renal crisis, which responds to ACE inhibitors.
Incorrect. Proton pump inhibitors are used for scleroderma-related esophageal reflux/GI symptoms, not for the renal crisis described here.
questions.overview: Diffuse systemic sclerosis carries early risk of visceral organ involvement, most dangerously scleroderma renal crisis, a life-threatening complication with acute renal failure and marked hypertension that responds to ACE inhibitors. This contrasts with limited scleroderma (CREST), where pulmonary disease rather than renal or cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death.

questions.stem: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria binds LPS-binding protein and then which macrophage surface receptor to trigger TLR4 signaling and cytokine release?
explanations: Incorrect. CD40 on B cells interacts with CD40 ligand on T cells to enable class switching, unrelated to LPS recognition on macrophages.
Correct. LPS bound to LPS-binding protein engages CD14 on macrophages, which triggers TLR4 signaling and production of cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF.
Incorrect. CD16 is the Fc receptor on NK cells that mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, not the LPS receptor on macrophages.
Incorrect. CD3 is part of the T-cell receptor signaling complex, not involved in LPS recognition by macrophages.
questions.overview: Innate immune cells recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) via pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs). LPS binds LPS-binding protein, then CD14 on macrophages, triggering TLR4 and cytokine production (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF), a key step in the innate response to gram-negative bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl presents with her third episode this year of nonpruritic swelling of her lips and face without urticaria, lasting 2-3 days and resolving spontaneously. Her father had similar episodes as a child. Laboratory testing reveals a low C4 level and low C1 inhibitor level. She is about to be started on an antihypertensive medication for newly diagnosed hypertension. Which class of medication should be avoided in this patient?
options: Calcium channel blockers, due to worsening of Raynaud phenomenon
ACE inhibitors, due to bradykinin accumulation and risk of life-threatening angioedema
Beta-blockers, due to risk of bronchospasm
explanations: Incorrect. Thiazide-induced hyperuricemia relates to gout risk, not to hereditary angioedema pathophysiology.
Incorrect. NSAID-induced gastric ulceration is a general risk but is not the specific, life-threatening contraindication relevant to hereditary angioedema, which is ACE inhibitor use.
Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers are not specifically dangerous in hereditary angioedema; the concern with Raynaud phenomenon applies to scleroderma, not this condition.

Correct. This is hereditary angioedema, caused by C1 inhibitor deficiency; because C1 inhibitor also normally breaks down bradykinin, its deficiency causes high bradykinin levels. ACE inhibitors, which also raise bradykinin (by blocking its breakdown), must never be given to these patients due to the risk of life-threatening angioedema.

Incorrect. While beta-blockers can worsen bronchospasm in some patients, this is not the specific life-threatening interaction described for hereditary angioedema; the critical contraindication is ACE inhibitors.
questions.overview: Hereditary angioedema is caused by deficiency of C1 inhibitor, a protein that normally breaks down bradykinin; deficiency leads to high bradykinin levels and recurrent episodes of nonpruritic swelling of skin, GI tract, and upper airway (potentially fatal) without urticaria. Diagnosis is supported by a low C4 level, and ACE inhibitors must never be given because they further raise bradykinin levels.

questions.stem: HLA-B27 positivity is found in approximately what percentage of patients with ankylosing spondylitis?
explanations: Incorrect. 50% is the approximate HLA-B27 positivity rate in psoriatic arthritis, not ankylosing spondylitis.
Incorrect. 10% underestimates the strong association between HLA-B27 and ankylosing spondylitis.
Correct. HLA-B27 is found in approximately 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis, the classic seronegative spondyloarthritis.
Incorrect. 25% is not the figure given in the notes for HLA-B27 association with ankylosing spondylitis.
questions.overview: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with the seronegative spondyloarthritides, being present in about 90% of ankylosing spondylitis patients and about 50% of psoriatic arthritis patients, although most HLA-B27-positive individuals never develop disease. Seronegative spondyloarthritis is characterized by asymmetric oligoarthritis, axial spine/sacroiliac involvement, dactylitis, and enthesitis, in contrast to the symmetric polyarthritis of rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with 6 months of low back pain that is worse at night and improves with movement, often awakening him from sleep. He also reports heel pain and swelling of several fingers. On examination there is decreased range of motion of the lumbar spine and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints. Laboratory studies show elevated ESR and CRP, and he tests positive for HLA-B27. If left untreated, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following extra-articular complications?
options: Pericarditis with pericardial effusion as the dominant cardiac finding
explanations: Correct. Ankylosing spondylitis can cause aortitis, which classically leads to aortic regurgitation, in addition to uveitis and restrictive lung disease from reduced chest wall and spinal mobility.
Incorrect. Libman-Sacks (marantic) endocarditis is a cardiac manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus, not ankylosing spondylitis.
Incorrect. Scleroderma renal crisis is a complication of diffuse systemic sclerosis, unrelated to ankylosing spondylitis.

Incorrect. Pericarditis is a described feature of rheumatoid arthritis and SLE serositis, not the classic extra-articular complication highlighted for ankylosing spondylitis, which is aortitis/aortic regurgitation.
Incorrect. Coronary artery aneurysm is the feared complication of Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis in children, not ankylosing spondylitis.
questions.overview: Ankylosing spondylitis is the classic seronegative spondyloarthritis, presenting with inflammatory back pain (worse with rest, improved with exercise), sacroiliitis progressing to a 'bamboo spine,' enthesitis (heel pain), and dactylitis. It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 (about 90% of cases) and can cause uveitis, aortitis leading to aortic regurgitation, and restrictive lung disease.

questions.stem: A patient receiving methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis develops significant myelosuppression. Which of the following can reverse this toxicity by bypassing the enzyme inhibited by methotrexate?
explanations: Correct. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; leucovorin (folinic acid) is converted directly to tetrahydrofolate without requiring this enzyme, providing 'leucovorin rescue' to reverse methotrexate-induced myelosuppression.
Incorrect. Mesna is used to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis from cyclophosphamide by inactivating its toxic metabolite acrolein; it has no role in reversing methotrexate toxicity.
Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is itself an immunosuppressant/alkylating agent, not a rescue therapy for methotrexate toxicity.

Incorrect. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for gout and to prevent tumor lysis syndrome; it does not reverse methotrexate myelosuppression and can dangerously interact with azathioprine/6-MP.
questions.overview: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidylate synthesis, causing myelosuppression and mucositis. Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses this block by being converted directly to tetrahydrofolate, allowing 'leucovorin rescue' from methotrexate toxicity.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with 6 months of progressively worsening pain and stiffness in both hands. She reports morning stiffness lasting more than an hour that improves with activity throughout the day. Examination shows symmetric swelling and tenderness of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints bilaterally, with sparing of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Laboratory studies show a positive rheumatoid factor, a positive anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA), and elevated ESR and CRP. Which of the following best describes the underlying immunologic mechanism causing joint destruction in this patient?
options: Deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes in the synovium with complement activation (type III hypersensitivity)
Direct cytotoxic antibody binding to synovial cell-surface antigens (type II hypersensitivity)
CD8+ T cell-mediated direct lysis of synoviocytes (type IV hypersensitivity)
Direct bacterial invasion and destruction of synovial tissue
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation within the joint space (type I hypersensitivity)
explanations: Correct. Rheumatoid arthritis is antibody-mediated and classified as a type III hypersensitivity reaction, with immune complexes depositing in the synovium, driving TNF and IL-6 overproduction, synovial hypertrophy (pannus), and erosion of cartilage and bone.

Incorrect. Type II hypersensitivity involves direct antibody binding to cell-surface or tissue antigens causing cytotoxicity (e.g., Goodpasture syndrome, myasthenia gravis), which is not the mechanism described for RA in the notes.
Incorrect. Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed, T-cell-mediated reaction without antibody involvement (e.g., PPD reaction, contact dermatitis), not the mechanism of RA.
Incorrect. RA is an autoimmune disorder, not an infectious process; there is no direct bacterial invasion of the synovium.
Incorrect. Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate IgE-mediated reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis) and does not describe RA pathogenesis.
questions.overview: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder causing symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis of the MCP and PIP joints (sparing DIP), driven by TNF and IL-6 overproduction and synovial pannus formation via a type III hypersensitivity mechanism. Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but nonspecific, while anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) are up to 80% sensitive and highly specific for RA and correlate with HLA-DR4.

questions.stem: A young boy has recurrent infections with Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, and Aspergillus, but not with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Nitroblue tetrazolium testing shows failure of neutrophils to turn blue. Which enzyme is deficient?
explanations: Correct. This is chronic granulomatous disease, caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency, which prevents the respiratory burst; the negative nitroblue tetrazolium test confirms lack of enzyme activity, and patients are susceptible to catalase-positive organisms like Staph aureus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, Nocardia, and Aspergillus (catalase-negative organisms such as S. pneumoniae generate their own H2O2 that phagocytes can still use).
Incorrect. Myeloperoxidase is contained in azurophilic granules and used within the phagosome, but its deficiency is not the defect tested by the nitroblue tetrazolium test described here.
Incorrect. Bruton tyrosine kinase deficiency causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia, an antibody deficiency, not a defect in the respiratory burst.
Incorrect. Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes a form of SCID via toxic dATP accumulation impairing lymphocyte function, unrelated to NADPH oxidase or the NBT test.
questions.overview: Chronic granulomatous disease results from NADPH oxidase deficiency, preventing the respiratory burst needed to generate hydrogen peroxide, leaving phagocytes unable to kill catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Pseudomonas, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus) since these organisms degrade their own H2O2; catalase-negative organisms are still handled because phagocytes can use the pathogen's own H2O2. Diagnosis is supported by a negative nitroblue tetrazolium test.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with 5 days of high fever. Examination reveals bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue with cracked lips, a diffuse erythematous rash, erythema and swelling of the hands and feet, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reduce the risk of the feared cardiac complication of this disease?
explanations: Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide with steroids is used for ANCA-associated vasculitides and polyarteritis nodosa, not Kawasaki disease.
Incorrect. High-dose corticosteroids alone are not the standard treatment for Kawasaki disease; IVIG and aspirin are used.
Incorrect. Smoking cessation is the treatment for Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), not applicable to a young child with Kawasaki disease.

Correct. This presentation is classic for Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood whose feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm; standard treatment is IV immunoglobulin plus aspirin (one of the few pediatric indications for aspirin, given the risk of Reye syndrome with viral illnesses).
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors are used for scleroderma renal crisis, not for Kawasaki disease.
questions.overview: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis occurring mainly in children, presenting with fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue/oral mucosal changes, extremity changes (later desquamation), rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Its feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm, which can rupture and cause myocardial infarction; treatment is IV immunoglobulin and aspirin.

questions.stem: Which pair of antibodies, when present in a pregnant woman with Sjögren's syndrome or SLE, is most associated with neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in the fetus?
explanations: Correct. Maternal anti-SSA (Ro) or anti-SSB (La) antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus, presenting with a rash and congenital complete heart block that often does not respond to steroids.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific for SLE but are not the antibodies described in the notes as causing neonatal lupus/congenital heart block.
Incorrect. Rheumatoid factor and ANA are nonspecific findings seen in multiple autoimmune diseases and are not specifically linked to neonatal lupus.
Incorrect. Anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70 are scleroderma-associated antibodies, unrelated to neonatal lupus.
questions.overview: Neonatal lupus results from transplacental transfer of maternal anti-SSA (Ro) or anti-SSB (La) antibodies, seen in mothers with SLE or Sjögren's syndrome, and can cause a rash and congenital complete heart block in the newborn, the latter often unresponsive to steroids.

questions.stem: Which cytokine, secreted primarily by macrophages, drives differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into the Th1 subset that mediates cellular immunity against intracellular pathogens?
explanations: Incorrect. IL-5 is a Th2 cytokine that activates eosinophils and promotes IgA production, not Th1 differentiation.
Incorrect. IL-4 is the major Th2 cytokine, promoting Th2 differentiation and IgE production, and suppressing Th1 responses—the opposite of what is described.
Incorrect. IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits Th1 production; it does not drive Th1 differentiation.
Correct. IL-12 from macrophages drives differentiation of CD4+ T cells into Th1 cells, which activate CD8 T cells and macrophages to fight intracellular pathogens such as M. tuberculosis.
questions.overview: CD4+ T cells differentiate into Th1 cells (cell-mediated immunity, driven by macrophage-derived IL-12, producing IFN-γ to activate macrophages and CD8 T cells) or Th2 cells (humoral immunity, driven by IL-4, promoting IgE/IgA antibody production via B cells). This balance is important in diseases such as tuberculosis (requires strong Th1) and leprosy (tuberculoid = Th1-dominant; lepromatous = Th2-dominant).

questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes IgA antibody function?
options: Binds mast cells to trigger degranulation against parasites
Crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus
Coats mucosal pathogens to prevent adherence without activating complement
Is the primary opsonin for encapsulated bacteria in the bloodstream
explanations: Incorrect. IgE, not IgA, binds mast cells and eosinophils and mediates defense against parasites and allergic reactions.
Incorrect. IgG, not IgA, is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the newborn.

Correct. IgA is the dominant antibody at mucosal surfaces (GI tract, respiratory tract, saliva, tears), coating pathogens to prevent invasion so they can be swept away; it does not fix complement, so it produces no inflammation.
Incorrect. IgG (especially IgG1 and IgG3) is the primary opsonin for encapsulated bacteria in the bloodstream; IgA does not fix complement and is a weak systemic opsonin.
questions.overview: IgA is the major antibody of mucosal immunity, secreted as a dimer linked by a joining segment and secretory component that allows transport across epithelial cells; it coats mucosal pathogens to block invasion without activating complement, avoiding local inflammation, and is also secreted into breast milk to protect the infant GI tract.

questions.stem: Glucocorticoids exert their anti-inflammatory effects in part by inactivating which key inflammatory transcription factor, thereby decreasing expression of COX-2, phospholipase A2, and other inflammatory mediators?
explanations: Incorrect. STAT3 is a signaling pathway activated by cytokines and is relevant to Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome) due to defective STAT3 signaling, not the mechanism of glucocorticoid action described here.

Correct. Glucocorticoids inactivate NF-κB, the key inflammatory transcription factor that mediates the response to TNF-α and controls synthesis of inflammatory mediators such as COX-2, phospholipase A2, and lipoxygenase.
Incorrect. NFAT is the transcription factor inhibited by calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), not by glucocorticoids.
Incorrect. HIF-1α is not the transcription factor targeted by glucocorticoids in this mechanism; it is not discussed in this context in the notes.
questions.overview: Glucocorticoids diffuse across the cell membrane and bind the glucocorticoid receptor, which translocates to the nucleus and inactivates NF-κB, a key transcription factor mediating TNF-α responses and inflammatory mediator synthesis (COX-2, phospholipase A2, lipoxygenase). This produces broad immunosuppressive effects but carries side effects such as osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, cataracts, myopathy, avascular necrosis, and adrenal insufficiency with abrupt discontinuation.

questions.stem: A patient presents with sinusitis, hemoptysis, and hematuria with red cell casts. Serologic testing is positive for antibodies against proteinase 3. Which vasculitis does this pattern most specifically indicate?
explanations: Incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa is not an ANCA-associated vasculitis; it is immune-complex mediated and associated with hepatitis B, affecting nerves, skin, and kidneys without pulmonary involvement.

Correct. c-ANCA, usually directed against proteinase 3 (PR3), is specific for granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), which presents with sinusitis, hemoptysis, and renal involvement with granulomas on biopsy.
Incorrect. Churg-Strauss syndrome is associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and p-ANCA (myeloperoxidase), not c-ANCA/PR3, and does not typically present with sinusitis.
Incorrect. Microscopic polyangiitis presents similarly but without sinusitis or granulomas, and is associated with p-ANCA (myeloperoxidase), not c-ANCA/PR3.
questions.overview: ANCA-associated vasculitides include granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3, sinusitis + pulmonary + renal disease with granulomas), microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA/MPO, pulmonary-renal without sinusitis or granulomas), and Churg-Strauss (p-ANCA/MPO, with asthma and eosinophilia). All three cause pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with minimal immunoglobulin deposition on immunofluorescence.

questions.stem: Which antibody test is most specific for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, targeting proteins modified by post-translational incorporation of a non-standard amino acid?
explanations: Correct. Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) target citrulline, a non-standard amino acid incorporated into proteins via post-translational modification during inflammation, and are a specific marker for RA (up to 80% of patients).
Incorrect. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is specific for diffuse systemic sclerosis, not rheumatoid arthritis.

Incorrect. Rheumatoid factor (antibody against the Fc portion of IgG) is present in about 80% of RA patients but has poor specificity, also occurring in endocarditis, hepatitis B/C, Sjögren's, and lupus.
Incorrect. ANA is a nonspecific marker seen in many autoimmune diseases, most notably SLE, and is not the specific test for RA.
questions.overview: Rheumatoid factor (anti-Fc IgG antibody) is present in ~80% of RA patients but is poorly specific, while anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) target citrulline—a non-standard amino acid incorporated into proteins during inflammation—and are a highly specific marker for RA, also present in up to 80% of patients.

questions.stem: A patient with SLE has an antibody whose titer fluctuates with disease flares and is associated with the development of lupus nephritis. Which antibody is this?
explanations: Incorrect. Anti-histone antibodies are the hallmark of drug-induced lupus, not a marker of disease activity or renal involvement in idiopathic SLE.
Incorrect. ANA is sensitive for SLE (present in nearly all patients) but is not specific and does not track with disease activity or renal involvement.
Correct. Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE, correlates with disease activity (rising with flares), and is associated with renal involvement (glomerulonephritis).
Incorrect. Anti-Sm is also specific for SLE but is not described as tracking with disease activity or specifically associated with renal flares.
questions.overview: In SLE, ANA is sensitive but not specific, while anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are both specific for the diagnosis. Anti-dsDNA additionally correlates with disease activity and flares and is associated with lupus nephritis, making it useful for monitoring disease.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops palpable purpura on his buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and melena one week after an upper respiratory infection. Which immunoglobulin mediates the vascular deposition underlying this condition?
explanations: Incorrect. IgM is important in the classical complement pathway and primary antibody responses but is not the immunoglobulin implicated in HSP.

Correct. Henoch-Schönlein purpura, the most common childhood systemic vasculitis, is caused by IgA immune complex deposition in vessel walls (along with C3), often following an upper respiratory infection, and can also cause IgA nephropathy.
Incorrect. IgE mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions such as anaphylaxis and allergic disease, not the vasculitis described in HSP.
Incorrect. IgG4 is not the antibody class described in the notes as mediating Henoch-Schönlein purpura.
questions.overview: Henoch-Schönlein purpura is the most common childhood systemic vasculitis, typically following an upper respiratory infection, and is mediated by IgA immune complex deposition in small vessels (with C3), causing palpable purpura on the buttocks/legs, abdominal pain with melena, and nephritis (overlapping with IgA nephropathy). It is usually self-limited, though renal failure is the feared outcome.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes a cadaveric renal transplant. Within minutes of reperfusion in the operating room, the graft becomes mottled and cyanotic, and urine output ceases. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for this finding?
options: Recipient CD8+ T-cell-mediated attack on donor cells
Recipient B-cell response generating new antibodies against donor antigens presented on MHC class II
Preformed recipient antibodies against donor ABO or HLA antigens
Donor T-cell attack against recipient tissues
Progressive fibrosis and vascular narrowing of the graft
explanations: Incorrect. CD8+ T-cell-mediated rejection describes acute rejection, which occurs weeks to months after transplant, not within minutes.

Incorrect. Generation of new antibodies takes time (days to weeks) and would not explain rejection occurring within minutes; hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-existing, not newly formed, antibodies.

Correct. This is hyperacute rejection, occurring within minutes of transplantation due to preformed recipient antibodies (from prior pregnancy, transfusion, or transplantation) against donor ABO or HLA antigens, causing vessel spasm, intravascular coagulation, and ischemia; it is prevented by cross-matching and is rare and usually untreatable once it occurs.
Incorrect. Donor T-cell attack on recipient tissue describes graft-versus-host disease, a complication of bone marrow transplantation, not hyperacute rejection of a solid organ.
Incorrect. Progressive fibrosis describes chronic rejection, which develops over months to years, not minutes.
questions.overview: Hyperacute transplant rejection occurs within minutes due to preformed recipient antibodies against donor ABO or HLA antigens, causing vessel spasm and intravascular coagulation ('white rejection'); it is prevented by cross-matching but is rare and generally not treatable. This contrasts with acute rejection (weeks-months, cell-mediated, treatable with immunosuppression) and chronic rejection (months-years, fibrosis).

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy, previously healthy, presents with recurrent otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia as maternal antibodies wane. Flow cytometry shows absent mature B cells (CD19+, CD20+) in peripheral blood, and serum immunoglobulins of all classes are markedly decreased. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
options: Failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches to develop
Mutation in the gamma chain of the interleukin-2 receptor
Mutation in the WAS gene affecting the T-cell cytoskeleton
Mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene preventing B-cell precursor maturation
Defective CD40 ligand expression on T cells
explanations: Incorrect. Failure of the third/fourth pharyngeal pouches causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia), which affects T cells and is associated with hypocalcemia and cardiac defects, not absent B cells.
Incorrect. IL2RG mutations cause X-linked SCID, which involves loss of both T-cell and (secondarily) B-cell/antibody function along with an absent thymic shadow, not isolated absent B cells.
Incorrect. WAS gene mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which presents with eczema, thrombocytopenia, and infections, not isolated absence of B cells with normal platelets.

Correct. This is X-linked (Bruton's) agammaglobulinemia, caused by a defect in the BTK gene that prevents B cell precursors from maturing into B cells, resulting in absent mature B cells and antibodies of all classes, with symptoms beginning around 6 months of age as maternal antibodies fade.

Incorrect. Defective CD40L causes Hyper-IgM syndrome, in which B cells are present but fail to class switch, producing elevated IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE rather than absent B cells and pan-hypogammaglobulinemia.
questions.overview: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's) results from a defect in the BTK gene that blocks B-cell precursor maturation into B cells, leading to absence of light chains and antibodies of all classes. It presents around 6 months of age, once maternal antibody protection wanes, with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections (otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia) and susceptibility to enteroviruses and Giardia; treatment is IVIG.

questions.stem: Which complement activation pathway is initiated by spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 to C3b, which is then stabilized on pathogen surfaces (such as bacterial LPS) by binding factors B and D?
explanations: Incorrect. The lectin pathway is initiated by mannose-binding lectin binding microbial surface mannose, not spontaneous C3 hydrolysis.

Correct. The alternative pathway begins with spontaneous conversion of C3 to C3b, which is normally rapidly destroyed unless stabilized on a pathogen surface by binding factors B and D to form C3 convertase (C3bBb), allowing rapid accumulation of C3b on the microbial surface.
Incorrect. The classical pathway is initiated by antibody-antigen complexes binding C1, not by spontaneous C3 hydrolysis.

Incorrect. The terminal (membrane attack complex) pathway is the common final step of all three pathways, formed from C5b through C9, and occurs downstream of C3 convertase formation, not as the initiating event.
questions.overview: All three complement pathways—classical (antibody-antigen via C1), lectin (mannose-binding lectin), and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis stabilized on pathogen surfaces by factors B and D)—converge on formation of C3 convertase, generating C3b that leads to the membrane attack complex (C5b-C9) and bacterial cell lysis. Host cells are protected from inappropriate complement activation by regulatory proteins such as Factor H, DAF (CD55), and CD59.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old obese man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe pain, redness, and swelling of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint that began after a large steak dinner accompanied by heavy alcohol consumption. Arthrocentesis reveals needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent under polarized light. His renal function is normal, and he has never had this problem before. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this acute episode?
explanations: Correct. This is an acute gout attack (podagra). First-line treatments for acute attacks include NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, or colchicine; NSAIDs are an appropriate first-episode choice in a patient with normal renal function.
Incorrect. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for chronic prevention of gout; starting it during an acute attack can abruptly change uric acid levels and precipitate or worsen a flare.
Incorrect. Probenecid is a uricosuric drug used for chronic prophylaxis, not for treating an acute attack.
Incorrect. Pegloticase is reserved for severe, refractory chronic gout, not for a first acute attack.
Incorrect. Aspirin is specifically noted as not used for pain control in gout; at low doses it can actually reduce uric acid excretion and worsen hyperuricemia.
questions.overview: Acute gout results from monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints (classically the first MTP joint, or podagra), producing needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on polarized microscopy. Acute attacks are treated with NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, or colchicine, while urate-lowering therapies (allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid, pegloticase) are used for chronic prevention and can precipitate attacks if started acutely without anti-inflammatory coverage.

questions.stem: Synovial fluid analysis in a 72-year-old man with acute knee pain shows rhomboid-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent under polarized light microscopy. This finding is most consistent with which condition?
explanations: Incorrect. Septic arthritis is diagnosed by identifying organisms and neutrophilic inflammation on culture/Gram stain, not crystal analysis.
Incorrect. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the light axis), not rhomboid and positively birefringent.
Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is diagnosed based on clinical features and serologic testing (RF, anti-CCP), not synovial fluid crystal analysis.

Correct. Pseudogout, caused by calcium pyrophosphate deposition, classically shows rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent crystals (blue when parallel to the light axis), commonly affecting the knee in older patients.
questions.overview: CPPD (pseudogout) typically occurs in older patients (average age 72) and produces rhomboid-shaped, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals on polarized light microscopy, in contrast to the needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals of gout. CPPD is associated with joint trauma, hyperparathyroidism, and hemochromatosis.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with sickle cell disease shows red blood cells containing small, round, basophilic nuclear remnants. This finding indicates which of the following?
options: Active bone marrow hemolysis only, with normal splenic function
explanations: Incorrect. Howell-Jolly bodies specifically reflect loss of splenic filtering function, not simply marrow hemolysis with a normally functioning spleen.

Correct. These are Howell-Jolly bodies, nuclear remnants normally removed by a functioning spleen; their presence in peripheral blood indicates splenic dysfunction, as occurs in functional asplenia from sickle cell disease.
Incorrect. Iron deficiency anemia is associated with microcytic, hypochromic red cells, not Howell-Jolly bodies, which reflect splenic dysfunction.
Incorrect. Howell-Jolly bodies are an abnormal finding indicating impaired splenic clearance, not a normal maturation feature.
questions.overview: The spleen normally filters and removes nuclear remnants from circulating red blood cells; when splenic function is lost (splenectomy, sickle cell-induced functional asplenia), Howell-Jolly bodies appear on peripheral smear. Splenic dysfunction also predisposes patients to overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms, most notably Streptococcus pneumoniae.
